fundamental.thesis: TCS is India's largest IT services company (₹8L cr market cap, near-debt-free with filing-reported D/E 0.099 and ROE 51%), serving global clients across BFSI (39.1% of revenue), Manufacturing, and Consumer verticals with dominant scale and 12-year consecutive top-ranked customer satisfaction. Revenue re-accelerated sharply in H1 FY27 to ₹1,45,463 cr (+12.6% YoY, with Q1FY27 at +13.9%), up from a sluggish +4.6% in FY26, and PAT margins expanded from 15.9% in Q3FY26 to 18.8% in H1 FY27 — but the critical flag is that FY26 constant-currency growth was -2.4%, meaning the INR headline re-acceleration is substantially FX-tailwind-driven (INR/USD ~94.96 vs ~84 in FY26) rather than evidence of genuine organic demand recovery; EBITDA margins have also contracted from 28.7% to 27.2%, and deferred revenue declined ₹1,092 cr QoQ, both pointing to margin and pipeline softening beneath the headline beat. At 16.3× trailing P/E — a 33.7% discount to the IT sector peer median of 24.7× and cheapest in sector on forward P/E at 13.4× — TCS screens unambiguously cheap versus both sector peers and the benchmark range of 22–30×, with a pristine balance sheet (CFO/PAT 0.94×, FCF ₹23,768 cr in H1) providing a durable floor; the P/E yardstick is used here as primary per the asset-light IT services model, and EV/EBITDA at 11.1× (P17 in sector vs median 14.7×) corroborates the cheap read. The central risk is AI-led productivity deflation continuing to compress legacy T&M revenues in constant-currency terms: if INR stabilises from current weakness, CC growth likely reverts to near-zero or negative, the INR acceleration collapses, and the re-rating catalyst disappears, leaving TCS cheap but with no near-term earnings growth to close the discount.

Q2FY27 consolidated revenue growth slowed to +5.0% and EBITDA fell 16% as cigarette net revenue dropped 21% and segment results dropped 27% after the tax increase, more than offsetting strength in non-cigarette revenue (+20%), FMCG Others (+19%), and paper (+36%); H1 PAT fell 17% to Rs 8,738 cr, implied Q2 PAT was about Rs 4,229 cr (roughly -16% YoY), and PAT margin fell from 24.8% in FY26 to about 13.8%, though that drop and the +35.5% H1 revenue growth look distorted because reported revenue likely includes higher excise. Using EV/EBITDA and P/E as a conglomerate yardstick, valuation is cheap at 12.1x EV/EBITDA and 16.9x trailing P/E versus FMCG medians of 34.6x and 51.5x, with filing-based TTM PAT of about Rs 18,654 cr implying closer to 18.8x, but the peer discount is only a partial guide because tobacco deserves a lower multiple than pure FMCG and estimates are being cut (FY EPS -5.1% over 90 days). The biggest risk is that cigarette profits have not yet bottomed, as legal volumes remain under pressure, so the low multiple could reflect a lasting earnings reset rather than a mispricing.

H1 FY27 revenue rose 31.0% YoY to Rs 100,575 cr, with growth building from +12.7% in Q2 FY26 through +17.0% (9M) and +20.2% (FY26), but this was unprofitable growth: PAT fell 18.3% to Rs 5,767 cr after +7.3%, +4.0% and +1.0%, and PAT margin dropped from about 8.2-8.3% to 5.7%, while average selling price stayed roughly flat (Rs 729,370 vs Rs 729,189 in Q2 FY26), so growth is coming from volume rather than pricing; the Q2 FY27 row is blank, the yfinance Q2 revenue of Rs 40,432 cr does not reconcile with H1, and the FY26, 9M and Q2 FY26 rupee figures appear to be understated tenfold, which I inferred from volumes x selling price and corrected only in the margin and trend reads. fundamental.thesis: Axis Bank is India's third-largest private-sector bank, with a large corporate and wholesale book, a growing retail franchise and a consolidated life-insurance associate (Axis Max Life). In Q2FY27, total income rose 14.8% YoY to ₹45,674 cr and PAT rose 39.4% to ₹7,705 cr. Revenue growth has picked up from about +4% (H1FY26) to +7% (Q1FY27) to +15%, and loan growth has risen from 11.9% to 19.3%, but the PAT jump is flattered by a weak Q2FY26 base (₹5,528 cr), and the PAT margin slipped from 17.7% in Q1 to 16.9%. On the lender yardstick from the sector card (P/B against sustainable ROE), a P/B of 1.83x for a TTM ROE of 13.2% is fair: it is above the peer median of 1.5x (P64), while trailing P/E of 15.0x is about 11% below peers (P43). That fits a bank whose asset quality has improved (GNPA down from 1.46% to 1.23%) but whose returns are only moderate. The biggest risk is that loans are now growing faster than deposits: the loan-to-deposit ratio is a stretched 98.7%, credit cost has risen from 0.20% to 0.72%, and provision coverage is slipping (70.5% to 70.0%). Together these point to future funding-cost and NIM pressure, and the extracted NIM readings (3.42% in Q1 vs 2.32% in Q2) conflict too much to confirm the NIM recovery the sector card expects.

Sun Pharma is India's largest drugmaker, with an 8.6% domestic market share (up 0.3pp), and also has US, emerging-market and innovative-medicines businesses. Q2 FY27 revenue growth improved to +11.8% from +10.1% in Q1, helped by India formulations growth of about +16.6% in H1, but US formulations fell 8.2% in Q2 after a 9.7% Q1 decline; H1 PAT fell 9.5% to Rs 4,883 cr, and adjusted PAT rose only about 2.2% on our unit-corrected reading (about Rs 6,252 cr, shown as Rs 62,515 cr in the feed), while EBITDA margin of 29.3% compares with 31.9% in the Q3 FY26 row, though the table's 'decelerating' signals mix non-comparable periods and should be read with caution. Using trailing P/E and peer rank, with EV/EBITDA as a cross-check, the stock is fair at 37.4x P/E, within the 28-40x sector range and close to the 36.4x peer median (P54), though EV/EBITDA of 24.2x is 13% above the peer median and FY EPS estimates have been cut 3.4% over 90 days despite 29 of 34 analysts rating it a buy. The biggest risk is the USD 14.0 bn Organon acquisition, which dwarfs net cash of about Rs 17,675 cr and will bring further costs, while H1 cash conversion is soft at 0.64x CFO/PAT and the content of the Assam facility news clarification is not in our data.

On valuation, we used the sector card's yardstick for premium discretionary franchises (normal band 60–100×) alongside EV/EBITDA. A trailing P/E of 74.3× and forward P/E of 49.4× sit inside the card's premium band, so we grade it fair overall, though not cheap. That premium is partly earned by a 37% ROE, and the peer median is pulled down by lower-multiple auto names. The biggest risk is that a growth disappointment at a 74× multiple can trigger the 25–40% de-rating the sector card warns about. That risk is higher in a risk-off market with rising crude and a falling gold price, which can hurt inventory gains and jewellery margins.

ONGC is India's largest oil and gas producer, and its earnings rise with crude prices, although government policy, including past windfall taxes, can limit the gain. The latest official standalone figures are for FY26, with revenue of ₹132,508 cr (-3.9% YoY) and PAT of ₹32,894 cr (-7.6% YoY); the cumulative revenue decline narrowed through the year from -9.4% in Q1 to -3.9% for the full year, so the 'decelerating' signal looks misleading, but PAT margin still slipped from 25.8% in FY25 to 24.8%, and no official Q1 FY27 figures are available, so the latest-quarter growth and margin fields are left null. Using EV/EBITDA and P/E plus dividend yield as the yardsticks, valuation is fair or policy-priced rather than clearly cheap: trailing P/E of 8.04x sits within the 6-10x PSU upstream norm and the 8-14x sector range, EV/EBITDA of 4.56x is 24.9% below the peer median at P33, and P/B is 0.9x with 12.7% ROE, while the 699% dividend yield and 42.55 debt/equity look like unit errors and the +25.8% target upside implies a price near ₹232 versus about ₹266 implied by the 46.6% 52-week position, so none of these three are relied on. The biggest uncertainty is that this view rests on stale numbers, with Q2 FY27 results due at the 5 November board meeting and the latest estimate revisions mixed (next-FY EPS -3.6% over 90 days), so conviction should stay low until the filing is reviewed.

fundamental.thesis: Dr Reddy's is a large Indian generics maker with heavy US exposure, plus a fast-growing India branded business and emerging-market and biosimilar franchises. In Q1 FY27 revenue fell 5.6% YoY to 8,070 cr, down from +3.0% in FY26, and PAT fell 69% to 435 cr (5.4% margin, down from 12.8%), partly because of a 223 cr semaglutide inventory provision. The biggest risk is that the US generics decline and the semaglutide delay keep hitting earnings before new launches can fill the gap.

On the sector-preferred P/E yardstick, trailing P/E of 37.9× sits at the P80 peer percentile and commands a 40% premium to the sector median of 27.1×; EV/EBITDA at 33.7× is P100 in its peer set and 84% above the sector median — on both measures the stock is expensive relative to peers, and the forward P/E of 28.8× (still P83) reflects already-priced-in earnings growth, leaving limited re-rating room. Using EV/EBITDA and trailing P/E alongside SSSG as the sector card suggests for retailers, valuation is expensive: EV/EBITDA of 55.3× is the highest among sector peers (P100, +152% vs the 21.9× median), and trailing P/E of 85.4× (P88) is within the card's 60-100× range but well above the 39.7× peer median, while the 55.8× forward P/E needs treating with caution because the gap to trailing could partly reflect the 1:2 bonus adjustment rather than earnings growth. The biggest risk is that a rich multiple meets slowing profit growth and softer operating signals, including inventory turnover down from 6.11× to 4.95× and debt service coverage down from 2.45× to 1.33×, with guidance only 'maintained' and a Chairman transition under way.

The biggest risk is that crude (USD 96.61 and rising) and a weak rupee keep costs above fares while softer passenger demand limits further fare increases, although Rs 39,929 cr of free cash provides a cushion against Rs 87,303 cr of debt including leases; the H1FY27 PAT and margin figures do not reconcile with Q1 and Q2, so this view relies on the quarterly numbers.

The biggest risk is that earnings depend heavily on lumpy investment gains while the lending subsidiaries face an Enforcement Directorate inquiry and a SEBI penalty with a 5-year market ban under appeal (next SAT hearing 30-Nov-2026), and no management guidance is available to improve visibility.

fundamental.thesis: Angel One is one of India's largest retail stockbrokers by active clients, so it earns mainly from broking fees (heavily F&O-linked), interest on client margin funding and distribution. That makes it a high-beta bet on market activity, not a lender. The latest extracted quarter is Q1FY27, where revenue rose +25.4% YoY to ₹1,430 cr and PAT doubled (+102%) to ₹231 cr, with PAT margin up from 10.0% to 16.2%. But this follows a weak FY26 (revenue -1.9%, PAT -21.9%), so much of the rebound is a recovery from a low base rather than proven new growth. The Q2FY27 results filed on 2026-10-15 are not yet in the extracted data. For a fee-based broker I graded on P/E cross-checked with P/B against ROE: trailing P/E of 35.8x is above the 18–28x NBFC/capital-markets band and in line with the broad market (P52), while forward P/E of 20.3x prices in a further earnings recovery. P/B of 5.25x against only 15.5% ROE is rich, so overall this is fair at best, with the stock at 97% of its 52-week range and FY EPS estimates cut 3.5% in 30 days and 4.8% in 90 days. The biggest risk is regulatory: further SEBI tightening of retail F&O, or a drop in market activity in this risk-off tape, would hit volumes directly. Cash flow from operations was also deeply negative in FY26 (-4.5x PAT) because the borrowed-money margin-funding book grew about 39%, which adds leverage (debt/equity about 1.0–1.3x).

Using P/B + ROE, the right yardstick for a bank, valuation is fair: 1.35× book is reasonable against an estimated 9-10% annualised Q2 ROE, but that return is below the 12% needed for a cheap grade, the 4.9% TTM ROE and 28.2× trailing P/E appear to reflect FY26 profit only, and the broad-market peer ranks are not a like-for-like bank comparison; price data also conflicts, since market cap and the 95.4% range position imply about ₹214 while the ₹187 target at +19.0% implies about ₹157. The biggest risk is funding, as advances grew 13.1% against deposits at 9.2% and CASA fell from 29.4% to 26.7%, with next-year EPS estimates also cut 4.2% over 90 days.

In Q2 FY27, net total income rose 58.9% YoY to ₹1,085 cr and PAT rose 77.3% to ₹418 cr, slowing from about +64% and +102% in Q1 but still very strong, while spread widened from 6.9% to 8.3% YoY and RoAE rose from 14.4% to 21.6%. On P/B versus ROE, the right yardstick for a lender, the stock is fair rather than cheap: P/B is 2.96× reported (about 2.7× on Q2 book value of ₹82.8) against TTM ROE of 16.5% and Q2 RoAE of 21.6%, with the price at 95% of its 52-week range limiting the margin of safety; trailing P/E of 21.84× is not used for the grade and appears stale against recent quarterly profits, the broad-market peer ranks are not a true lender comparison, and the 9.0% dividend yield looks unreliable. The biggest risk is that very rapid growth is beginning to strain asset quality and capital: GNPA rose from 1.1% to 1.2% QoQ, net NPA from 0.6% to 0.8%, provision cover fell from 43.2% to 33.3%, and CRAR fell from 32.9% to 22.7% YoY.

At trailing P/E of 28.2× (above the 12–22× Materials sector median but at P38 in the broad market, below the 35.2× broad-market median) and EV/EBITDA of 17.36× (P32 vs a 23.3× broad-market median), the stock grades as fairly valued — forward P/E of 21.47× is a meaningful discount to trailing, confirming consensus expects earnings to continue growing, and the 30/90-day EPS revision of +6.6% is supportive. The primary risk is elevated Debt/Equity of 2.91× in a rising crude ($90.41/bbl) and weakening INR (96.05/USD) environment, which could pressure chemical input costs and unwind the margin recovery if the Performance segment's volume momentum decelerates.

fundamental.thesis: Gland Pharma is a mid-cap injectables maker: it develops and manufactures injectable drugs for partners (B2B) and makes them to order for other drug companies (CDMO). It sells mainly into the US, where Q1 FY27 revenue rose 32% YoY to ₹981 cr, and owns the European CDMO Cenexi. In Q1 FY27 consolidated revenue was ₹1,800 cr, up 20% YoY, and PAT was ₹317 cr, up 47% YoY, for a PAT margin of 17.6%. Revenue growth has picked up from +6–7% a year ago to +20–23% over the last three quarters, and PAT margin has widened from 12–14% to about 18%, though revenue grew only 3% and PAT fell 14% versus Q4. Using the pharma P/E yardstick, a trailing P/E of 35.3x is inside the 28–40x sector range and at the median of its broad-market peers (P50). EV/EBITDA of 20.1x and P/B of 3.5x are below the peer median, and the forward P/E of 24.1x prices in continued growth, so overall valuation is fair, not cheap. The stock also sits at 76% of its 52-week range. Management raised its medium-term growth target to about 20% CAGR from 15% and estimates are up 5–7% over 90 days, but the biggest risks are that the strong US growth slows (the US is reviewing whether generic drugs should also face tariffs) and an overhang from a promoter-side Fosun shareholding disclosure that arrived alongside a board change, ahead of Q2 results on 6 Nov.

fundamental.thesis: MRPL is a PSU mid-cap refinery (ONGC subsidiary) processing ~4.4 MMT/quarter of crude at Mangalore, operating in a policy-administered margin environment where GRMs, not crude price alone, drive earnings. H1FY27 revenue surged +67.6% YoY to ₹77,199 cr and PAT exploded +697.6% YoY to ₹2,846 cr (PAT margin 3.7%), a dramatic recovery from the near-zero-profit FY26 base (PAT margin 1.8%), with EBITDA margin expanding to 6.6% on strong throughput and higher product realisations — though a fire incident at the CHT unit on 30-Sep-2026 provisionally cost ₹118 cr and creates near-term operational uncertainty. Using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick for this capital-intensive refinery (per sector card guidance for PSU OMCs/refiners), MRPL trades at 5.97× EV/EBITDA versus a broad-market median of 23.3× — placing it at P3 in its peer universe — making it structurally cheap, though the sector card explicitly cautions this discount is 'policy-priced' (permanent policy risk, not a valuation error); trailing P/E of 14.5× sits at the upper end of the PSU OMC range (6–10× + yield), but the forward P/E collapses to 3.4×, implying the street is pricing in a very strong FY27 full-year earnings recovery. The key risk is that elevated crude at $97.97/bbl directly compresses refining marketing margins for OMC-adjacent refiners, estimate revisions are sharply negative (-9.6% 30d, -21.2% next-FY 90d) signalling analyst concern about GRM sustainability, and the CHT fire adds operational/insurance settlement uncertainty over the next 1–2 quarters.

fundamental.thesis: Castrol India is the market-leading branded lubricants company, with a 167,000-outlet distribution network that grew its rural reach to 46,000 outlets, so it behaves more like a consumer-brands business than the oil PSUs in the Energy sector card. For 9M CY26, revenue rose 20.3% YoY to ₹5,151 cr but PAT grew only 8.7% to ₹766 cr; backing out H1 (₹3,417 cr revenue, ₹590 cr PAT) implies the Sep-quarter revenue grew about 27% to roughly ₹1,734 cr while PAT fell about 22% to roughly ₹176 cr, so PAT margin dropped from 18.6% in the Jun quarter to about 10%, and the implied EBITDA margin of about 15% sits well below management's 21-24% target band. Using EV/EBITDA and P/E as the yardstick (not the PSU 'policy-priced' P/E-plus-yield framework), the stock trades at 17.7x trailing P/E and 11.9x EV/EBITDA, about 50% below the broad-market median (P18/P17), but trailing earnings include the stronger H1 and FY-EPS estimates were cut 4.9% over 30 days, so I grade it fair rather than cheap until margins stabilise. The biggest risk is that crude above $100 and a rupee at 95 per dollar keep raising base-oil costs faster than the company's low double-digit price hikes can pass them through, while weak cash conversion (CFO/PAT 0.52x in H1) suggests working capital is soaking up the growth.

LT Foods is a midcap FMCG company that owns the Daawat rice brand, but its roughly 11% EBITDA margin is far from a typical premium staples profile. The Q2 FY27 numbers were filed on 2026-10-27 but were not extracted, so the latest usable quarter is Q1 FY27: revenue was Rs 3,161 cr (+26.0% YoY), with growth steady at about 24-26% across recent periods (the pre-computed 'decelerating' signal relies on a faulty Q2 FY26 row), while PAT was only Rs 183 cr (+9.0%) on a 5.8% margin, and gross margin fell from 34.4% in 9M FY26 to 32.6%. On trailing P/E of 21.5x, against an FMCG norm of 40-65x, and EV/EBITDA of 10.4x (P11 against a broad-market fallback, not close peers), the stock grades cheap, though the sector card warns that cheap FMCG often signals a structural problem, the 13.3x forward P/E implies earnings growth well above the current PAT trend, and the 7.5x P/B, 105% dividend yield and 28.49 debt/equity look unreliable and were given no weight. The main risk is that sales growth of 12% volume plus 11% price/mix keeps failing to reach profit, as in FY26 when revenue rose 26.1% but PAT only 2.2%, although cash conversion was sound at 1.46x CFO/PAT with FCF of Rs 551 cr.

Using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick for this capital-intensive PSU upstream business (sector card guidance), OIL trades at 8.31× EV/EBITDA and a trailing P/E of 10.33× — marginally above the sector card's PSU upstream range of 6–10× but forward P/E collapses to 6.86×; ranked P7 percentile (bottom cohort) across 473 peers on all metrics, making it clearly cheap in relative terms. ACME Solar is a leveraged renewable power producer with about 2,990 MW operating and 5,080 MW under construction as of Q1 FY27, and it is adding battery storage (BESS), with long-term PPAs on its pipeline. H1 FY27 revenue rose 78.2% YoY to Rs 1,745 cr and PAT rose 105% to Rs 504 cr, compared with Q1 growth of +63.3% and +79.9%, which implies faster growth in Q2, including PAT of about Rs 269 cr, but the pre-computed trajectory signals mix H1, Q1 and full-year periods and clean Q2 revenue and margin are left null because Q1 and H1 revenue definitions appear inconsistent (implied Q2 EBITDA exceeds implied revenue, and the 97.7% H1 EBITDA margin looks inflated). Using EV/EBITDA as the yardstick for this capital-intensive business, 15.15x is fair rather than cheap: it sits at P26 against a broad-market fallback set rather than true peers, trailing P/E of 40.7x looks stale (about 31x on my estimate of TTM PAT near Rs 756 cr), 13.7x forward P/E assumes profit more than doubles, and the stock is at 80.5% of its 52-week range; the snapshot also conflicts internally, since market cap and range imply a price near Rs 332 while the consensus upside implies about Rs 413, so the +16.6% upside and 6.0% dividend yield should not be relied on. The biggest risk is funding the build-out, with H1 free cash flow of Rs -5,263 cr on Rs 6,329 cr capex, debt/equity of about 3.9x and interest coverage of only 2.47x, while H1 operating cash flow of Rs 1,067 cr (2.12x PAT) is solid but covers only a small part of capex.

fundamental.thesis: Bata India is India's largest branded footwear retailer (~1,500 stores), competing in mid-to-premium segments where D2C and unorganized competition are intensifying. FY26 revenue was flat at ₹3,530 cr (+0.6% YoY) with H1FY26 decelerating to −2.2%; PAT fell 59.5% to ₹134 cr — partly one-off distorted (FY25 land sale gain of ₹134 cr absent + FY26 VRS/labour costs of ₹49 cr) — but EBITDA margins genuinely compressed from 26.5% (FY25) to 20.9% (FY26), confirming real operating deleverage and not merely a base-effect story. On EV/EBITDA (13.69×, P22 vs broad market, 41% discount to median), the stock screens cheap on operating metrics; however, trailing P/E of 75.6× with ROE of only 8.5% and P/B of 6.43× reflects poor capital productivity — we grade valuation 'fair' using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick per sector card guidance, noting the forward P/E of 37× already prices in a full earnings recovery that ongoing sell-side estimate cuts (−5.8% over 90 days) do not yet support. Three SMP/KMP changes in September 2026 alone raise governance and strategic continuity concerns at precisely the juncture when a clear management reset is most needed.

Emcure Pharmaceuticals is a mid-sized drugmaker selling branded medicines in India and overseas, with international markets (Europe, Canada and Rest of World) now 57.6% of revenue. Q1 FY27 revenue rose 22.8% YoY to Rs 2,580 cr and PAT rose 36.2% to Rs 292 cr, with revenue growth accelerating from +13.4% in Q2 FY26 and +20.4% in Q3 FY26, and EBITDA margin edging up from 19.2% to 19.7% over the past year, although domestic growth lagged at 10.2% and gross margin fell 340 bps to 58.4%. On trailing P/E, the main yardstick, valuation is fair at 37.1x, within the 28-40x pharma range but towards its upper end, with EV/EBITDA of 20.3x and forward P/E of 25.5x as cross-checks; the stock sits at 91% of its 52-week range, which limits upside, and the peer ranks are only a broad-market comparison, while the 18% dividend yield looks like a data error and the 30.57 debt/equity reading is probably a percentage (about 0.31x), not high leverage. The biggest risk is that growth is coming from lower-margin international business, and this view excludes the Q2 FY27 results scheduled for board approval today and the 2 October regulatory order, whose contents were not provided, while no FDA status was disclosed in the Q1 filing.

fundamental.thesis: CONCOR is India's dominant rail container logistics PSU (~70% share in rail containerisation), operating EXIM and domestic freight corridors with an embedded structural role in India's trade infrastructure. Revenue growth decelerated to near-zero in Q1FY27 (+0.3% YoY on ₹2,160 cr) continuing a multi-quarter stagnation (Q1FY26: +2.4%, FY25: +2.7%), with PAT essentially flat at +0.1% YoY and EBITDA/PAT margins contracting to 24.5%/12.3% from their 9M FY26 peaks of 26.4%/14.4% — the Domestic segment is structurally weak at a 4.14% PBIT margin and -3.5% volume decline. Using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick for this capital-intensive logistics infrastructure business, CONCOR trades at 14.2× — a 39% discount to the broad-market median of 23.3× (P23 percentile), with trailing P/E of 28.5× at the lower bound of the Industrials sector range (28–45×), grading as fair rather than cheap because ROE of 9.8% (below cost of equity) and a very high D/E of 7.39 undermine the P/B multiple case. The single biggest risk is management's bullish FY27 guidance (18% overall growth driven by DFC-JNPA connectivity and assured transit trains) having zero support from Q1 execution, compounded by an unquantified Land License Fee liability with Railways and a governance non-compliance flag (only 1 independent director as of June 2026), both of which create PSU-specific overhang that sell-side estimate cuts (-9.2% in 30 days, -10.5% in 90 days) are beginning to price in.

Carborundum Universal makes abrasives, ceramics and electrominerals, and has standalone operations plus overseas subsidiaries, several of which are now troubled. Q2 FY27 revenue rose 13.1% YoY to Rs 1,455 cr, easing from +17.0% in Q1 but well above the low-single-digit growth of FY26, while reported PAT fell 83.4% to Rs 12 cr (0.9% margin) because of an Rs 80.26 cr charge to wind down the German subsidiary; profit before exceptional items rose 22.1% to Rs 138 cr, led by Ceramics (+36.1%), but core Abrasives grew only 4.0% and Electrominerals profit fell 21.2%. On EV/EBITDA, the main yardstick for this business, the stock looks expensive at 34.5x, which is 47.9% above the broad-market median and at P72, and although the 115.3x trailing P/E is inflated by one-offs and the 40.1x forward P/E sits inside the 28-45x sector range, that forward multiple already assumes a sharp recovery with the stock at 85.8% of its 52-week range, ROE at 4.4%, and 4 of 6 analysts rating it a sell. The biggest risk is that the earnings recovery falls short while problems continue at the overseas subsidiaries, with Germany closing, South Africa on a non-going-concern basis and Russia's VAW on the US OFAC sanctions list; order-book data and guidance were unavailable, the peer set is a broad-market fallback, and the 38.0% dividend yield, 10.29 debt/equity and Rs 10,413 cr VAW impairment look like data errors and were not relied on.

Using EV/EBITDA as the primary multiple for capital-intensive industrials (per sector card), FINCABLES at 22.76× sits at the broad-market median (P49 peer rank, -2.4% vs median), while trailing P/E of 24.84× is modestly below the Industrials sector benchmark lower bound of 28×; the stock is at 94.6% of its 52-week range with analyst consensus mean target implying -0.7% from current price, pointing to fair — not cheap — valuation. Escorts Kubota is a mid-sized Indian tractor maker with a smaller construction equipment arm; agri machinery is about 85% of H1 revenue, so it behaves more like a farm-cycle manufacturer than an order-book Industrials name. Subtracting Q1 from H1 implies Q2 FY27 revenue of about Rs 3,243 cr, up 16.2% YoY (slowing from +28.3% in Q1), and PAT of about Rs 250 cr, a 7.7% margin against 12.0% in Q1; PAT fell about 21% against the reported Rs 318 cr, though it looks roughly flat if the prior-year land-sale gain sits in that quarter, and the reported H1 PAT drop of 62.9% mostly reflects the earlier railway business sale, with continuing PAT up only 2.2%. Using EV/EBITDA and P/E as the yardsticks because order-book measures do not fit this business, valuation looks fair rather than cheap at 16.3x EV/EBITDA and 22.6x trailing P/E: it is below the 28-45x Industrials range but inside the 18-28x Auto range that better suits a tractor maker, the P28-P30 peer ranks are against the broad market rather than close peers, and the 19.8x forward P/E rests on FY estimates already cut 11.6%. The main risk is that revenue growth is not reaching profit or cash, with agri EBIT margin down 340 bps to 9.3%, H1 operating cash flow at -Rs 107 cr on an inventory and receivables build, and management's margin recovery from Q4 dependent on stable commodity costs while crude is rising; the Rs 698 cr net cash cushions this, but the 1.31 debt/equity reading conflicts with it, and the 117% dividend yield, H1 EBITDA margin comparisons and +30.8% consensus upside also look unreliable, so none of them were relied on.

fundamental.thesis: GRSE is India's premier PSU defence shipbuilder with a ₹50,000 cr order book (~7× FY26 revenues of ₹7,002 cr), providing exceptional multi-year revenue visibility backed by the government's defence indigenisation drive and growing capital procurement allocations. Q1FY27 revenue grew 38.5% YoY to ₹1,815 cr and PAT grew 43.8% YoY to ₹173 cr, sustaining a consistently strong 30–49% growth pattern across 6 periods, though EBITDA margins have contracted from 14.9% (FY25) to 13.7% (Q1FY27) and guidance has only been 'maintained' twice — no upgrades despite the execution strength. Using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick for this capital-intensive shipbuilder, 29.34× sits within the 28–45× Industrials range but at P65 vs the broad market, rendering valuation fair; the forward P/E of 27.33× at a meaningful discount to trailing 34.84× confirms analysts expect continued EPS growth, while the P/B of 10.59× (P84 vs peers) signals the PSU defence franchise premium is already well-embedded at current prices. The critical risk is severely negative cash conversion — CFO/PAT was –0.39× in FY26 and –2.21× in H1FY26 — driven by trade receivables turnover collapsing from 17.91× to 6.27×, indicating government client payment delays that are building acute working capital stress and could erode the currently pristine near-zero debt balance sheet if collections do not normalise.

Q2 FY27 revenue was Rs 1,189 cr, with growth slowing from +25.4% in Q3 FY26 to +23.3% in Q1 FY27 and +18.3% now, while PAT of Rs 180 cr gives a 15.2% margin (the table shows 14.9%) against 17.9% in Q3 FY26, and EBITDA margin is 25.4% against 27.7%, up only slightly from 24.6% in Q1; no Q2 PAT growth figure is available, but H1 EPS growth of +8.4% against Q1 PAT growth of +16.0% suggests Q2 was only about +2% (my rough estimate). Using trailing P/E and EV/EBITDA, the stock looks cheap at 19.5x trailing P/E against the 22-30x IT services range and 12.0x EV/EBITDA (P18 against a broad-market peer set, not close competitors), though the 15.01 debt/equity reading conflicts with the reported net cash position and looks unreliable, and H1 cash figures also conflict, so I place little weight on either. The low multiple may be justified rather than a mispricing, because FY EPS estimates have been cut 5.5% in 30 days and 7.9% in 90 days, and a further slowdown or margin squeeze would shrink the earnings the valuation rests on.

fundamental.thesis: Wockhardt is an Indian specialty pharma company that has pivoted away from US generics (exited July 2025) toward a proprietary novel antibiotic pipeline anchored by Zaynich (FDA-approved May 2026) and India branded formulations, with 28 subsidiaries across multiple geographies and ₹32,323 cr market cap. Q1FY27 consolidated revenue grew +25.9% YoY to ₹929 cr (vs ₹738 cr), PAT swung from a ₹90 cr loss to ₹106 cr profit, and EBITDA margin expanded sharply to 24.0% vs 13.7% a year prior — a genuine turnaround, but these metrics are substantially inflated by the deeply negative Q1FY26 base, and domestic formulations growth at ~21% is the more reliable read on underlying demand momentum. Trailing P/E of 152.43× sits at P98 vs 499 market peers (333% premium to broad-market median 35.2×) and far exceeds the pharma sector median of 28–40×; EV/EBITDA of 52.4× (P90 vs peers) paired with P/B of 6.53× against a meagre 4.0% ROE signals the market is pricing in significant Zaynich pipeline success — graded expensive using EV/EBITDA as primary yardstick per the sector card for capital-intensive specialty pharma. The biggest risk is that extraordinary debt/equity of 42.28 with ₹52 cr in quarterly finance costs leaves minimal margin of safety — any delay in Zaynich commercialization or continued mixed subsidiary performance (18 of 28 subsidiaries unreviewed; 5 audited reporting a net ₹2 cr loss on ₹777 cr revenue) could strain free cash flow and force dilutive capital raises.

Rainbow runs a 26-hospital children's and women's care network with 2,555 beds, of which 1,910 are operational; paediatrics is 65% of its mix and 63.3% of patients pay cash. Q2FY27 revenue rose 23.2% YoY to Rs 548 cr, up from +6.5% in Q2FY26 and +11.9% in Q3FY26 (Q4FY26 and Q1FY27 are missing), but PAT rose only 10.9% to Rs 84 cr as EBITDA margin fell from 33.5% to 31.0% and PAT margin from 17.0% to 15.3%, likely partly because new hospitals are at 27.4% occupancy and a -16% EBITDA margin. Using EV/EBITDA as the main yardstick for a capital-intensive hospital chain, valuation is fair at 26.1x (12% above the median, P59), though this comparison is against the broad market rather than hospital peers and the 51.3x trailing P/E and 36.5x forward P/E (P77) leave limited room for error; the 24% dividend yield looks like a data error and was ignored, and the consensus target's +37.1% upside implies a price of about Rs 1,241 against about Rs 1,445 implied by the 52-week position, so it was not relied on. The biggest risk is that growth keeps costing margin: FY-EPS estimates are down 5% over 30 and 90 days despite 13 of 14 analysts rating it a buy, and group occupancy is only 49.2%.

fundamental.thesis: ABFRL is India's largest fashion and lifestyle retailer with 1,286 stores across four segments — Pantaloons (value/mass retail, 399 stores, 15.9% EBITDA margin), ethnic brands (672 stores, near-zero 0.1% EBITDA margin), TMRW (D2C digital-first, 75 stores, -19.2% EBITDA margin), and luxury/others (52 stores, 10% EBITDA margin) — competing in an intensely capital-intensive, multi-format environment. Q1 FY27 consolidated revenue grew a stable +10.6% YoY to ₹2,026 cr with EBITDA margin expanding to 8.2% (vs 5.9% full-year FY26), a genuine operational improvement, but PAT losses deepened to ₹-249 cr (-6.4% worse YoY, -12.3% margin) as TMRW's ₹-42 cr EBITDA drag and ethnic segment's near-zero margins overwhelm Pantaloons' solid contribution; revenue growth has been remarkably steady at 10-11% across periods, but PAT trajectory is deteriorating not improving. P/E is inapplicable given persistent losses; using EV/EBITDA (18.2×, a 22% discount to broad-market peer median 23.3×) and P/Sales (0.92×, below 1 for a consumer brand) valuation appears statistically cheap, but with FY26 FCF of ₹-348 cr, D/E of ~99× (including lease liabilities), and negative interest and debt-service coverage, the discount reflects quality and solvency risk rather than a mispricing — graded fair. The single biggest risk is a prolonged path to PAT profitability: TMRW burns ~₹42 cr EBITDA per quarter with a -19.2% margin (improving by only ₹21 cr YoY), free cash flow is deeply negative, and any revenue deceleration or credit-market tightening could force dilutive equity issuance from a near-52-week-low stock price.

Syngene is a mid-sized Indian contract research and manufacturing company serving global pharma, with capacity in India and a newly acquired US biologics site. H1FY27 revenue rose 13.1% YoY to Rs 1,629 cr and PAT rose from Rs 46.6 cr to Rs 140 cr (8.6% margin), but this followed a Q1 revenue decline of 17.1% and a small loss, while FY26 revenue grew only 2.6% and PAT fell 36.1%; the implied Q2 rebound is unproven because the mixed-period trend table, the yfinance rows and the implied H1FY26 base do not reconcile, so the table's 'accelerating' and 'contracting' labels are unreliable. Using EV/EBITDA as the main yardstick for this capital-intensive model, valuation is fair at 17.35x (P32 and 25.6% below the median, but against a broad-market peer set rather than true CDMO peers), while the 69.95x trailing P/E is inflated by depressed and inconsistently reported earnings and the 36.03x forward P/E still needs a strong recovery. The biggest risk is that the price near its 52-week low (2.9% of range) is a falling knife rather than value: FY EPS estimates were cut 21.1% in the last 30 days, H1 operating cash flow was -Rs 143 cr, FCF was -Rs 363 cr, and restructuring costs and a management change add execution risk.

fundamental.thesis: Devyani International is India's largest QSR franchisee by store count (2,255 stores), operating KFC, Pizza Hut, and Costa Coffee alongside own brands (Biryani By Kilo, Vaango), with a pending merger with Sapphire Foods targeting completion by end-FY27. Q1FY27 revenue grew 16.5% YoY to ₹1,580 cr — holding steady from prior-quarter acceleration — with PAT turning positive at ₹17 cr (1.1% margin) driven by KFC (+3.3% SSSG, +38% operating EBITDA YoY) and own brands, but badly offset by Pizza Hut India which collapsed -24.9% YoY with 13 net store closures and SSSG of -1.9% for a second consecutive negative quarter. Using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick for this Ind AS 116-heavy QSR (per sector card guidance on capital-intensive businesses), 21.06× sits near the broad-market peer median (P45), which might suggest fair, but reported EBITDA is inflated by ₹103.7 cr of lease-accounting treatment vs. operating EBITDA of only ₹151 cr (9.6% margin); the 103× forward P/E at P100 vs. all peers, a negative ROE of -2.6%, and D/E of 203× collectively signal the market is pricing in flawless execution of the Sapphire merger and a Pizza Hut turnaround management itself only expects in FY28. The biggest structural risk is that Pizza Hut's decline deepens post-merger integration while high finance costs (₹70 cr/quarter, 4.4% of revenue) keep PAT margins razor-thin, with sell-side EPS estimates already revised down -8.4% over 90 days despite a still-bullish analyst mix — a classic pre-derating pattern.

Aditya Birla Lifestyle Brands owns a large branded-apparel retail business with 3,434 stores, led by its lifestyle brands (19.5% EBITDA margin) and supported by a faster-growing but lower-margin emerging portfolio (6.8%). Q2FY27 revenue rose 11.0% YoY to Rs 2,266 cr, up from +3.7% in Q2FY26 and +9.6% in Q3FY26, while PAT rose about 126% to Rs 53 cr off a low base, with PAT margin at 2.3% (1.1% a year ago, 2.9% in Q3FY26) and like-for-like retail growth at a moderate 5.3%; Q4FY26 and Q1FY27 are missing from the trend, so this is not an unbroken trajectory. Using EV/EBITDA plus retail like-for-like growth as the yardstick, valuation is fair: 15.9x EV/EBITDA is at P28 against a broad-market median of 23.3x, while the 58.1x trailing P/E (P76) is inflated by thin profit margins, and the 27.2x forward P/E assumes earnings roughly double. The biggest risk is that this earnings recovery falls short, because thin margins leave little cushion if festive or urban demand weakens, and the price near its 52-week low (2.4% of range) with FY-EPS estimates cut 1.7% over 30 days shows the market is not yet convinced.

Revenue growth has improved from -2.9% in Q3 FY26 to +9.3% in Q1 FY27 and +14.0% to Rs 3,875 cr in H1 FY27, while H1 PAT rose 40.1% to Rs 604 cr and implied Q2 (H1 minus Q1, not a reported figure) shows revenue of about Rs 1,905 cr (+15%) and PAT of about Rs 345 cr (+58%, 18.1% margin), though the filing data conflict on Q1 growth and on the H1 FY26 EBITDA margin (18.4% vs 20.1%), so these Q2 figures are approximate. Revenue growth swung from +13.0% in Q1 FY27 (Rs 1,458 cr) to about -27.7% in Q2 (about Rs 940 cr vs Rs 1,300 cr, derived as H1 minus Q1), while H1 revenue fell 7.4% to Rs 2,398 cr and H1 PAT rose 11.3% to Rs 984 cr; Q2 PAT was up only about 3% at about Rs 365 cr, and the core business looks soft, with Q2 advertising down 13.5% and subscriptions up just 2.3%, although lumpy cricket income, not split by quarter here, may overstate the revenue drop. On EV/EBITDA of 4.6x (P2 against a broad-market peer set, as there are no close peers and the card's 60-100x norms do not fit a broadcaster), backed by trailing P/E of 12.25x and P/B of 1.48x, the stock grades cheap near the bottom of its 52-week range, though some discount is deserved for a shrinking ad business; I ignored the 445% dividend yield and the +12.6% target upside as they do not match the roughly Rs 476 price implied by market cap and 52-week position, and I did not rely on the EBITDA margin trend because its period figures do not reconcile. fundamental.thesis: Deepak Fertilisers is a mid-cap ammonia-chain business. It makes industrial chemicals (nitric acid, IPA, methanol), it is a leading Indian producer of technical ammonium nitrate (TAN) for mining, and it sells crop nutrition (NPK, specialty fertilisers), with large new capacity at Gopalpur (TAN) and Dahej (nitric acid) due to start in Q2 FY27. On the official filings, FY26 revenue grew 12.0% to ₹11,506 cr, but PAT fell 21.8% to ₹739 cr. Profitability has been shrinking through the year: PAT margin slid from 8.1% (H1) to 7.0% (9M) to 6.4% (full year), and EBITDA margin from 17.3% to 14.6%. The filing-extracted trend table has no Q1 FY27 revenue or PAT, and the unverified yfinance figure (PAT ₹490 cr on ₹1,886 cr revenue) looks like it may include a one-off. Treating this as a cyclical chemicals business, we judge it on EV/EBITDA: 11.1× is about half the broad-market median (bottom 15% of the market), but it is above the 5–8× the sector card calls normal for chemical cyclicals at mid-cycle. Trailing P/E of 16.9× sits inside the 12–22× Materials range, so overall we grade it fair. The forward P/E of 10.6× and analysts raising this year's earnings estimates by 43% over 30 days already assume the new plants succeed. The biggest risks are a slow ramp-up at the new plants with debt high (debt/equity about 0.76) and free cash flow negative (−₹396 cr in H1 FY26), together with raw-material squeeze from the Middle East and a falling-margin trend.

Dalmia Bharat is a mid-sized Indian cement maker with 54.7 MTPA installed capacity across 12 states, expanding toward 67 MTPA, including the acquired Jaypee assets in Central India. Q2FY27 revenue, derived as H1 minus Q1 because the Q2 row is blank, was about ₹3,563 cr (+4.3% YoY, slowing from +10.7% in Q2FY26), and PAT was about ₹-201 cr after ₹339 cr of exceptional items; volume rose only 3%, EBITDA per tonne fell from ₹1,013 to ₹746, below the ₹900-1,100 healthy range, and management expects more fuel and Central India cost pressure in Q3. On the capital-intensive yardsticks of EV/EBITDA and EBITDA per tonne, I grade valuation fair: 12.3x EV/EBITDA is on depressed earnings, the 35.0x trailing P/E (Materials benchmark 12-22x) is distorted by one-offs, and the P19 EV/EBITDA and P15 P/B ranks are less useful because they compare against the broad market, not cement peers; the 15.7% position in the 52-week range offers some support, but this is not clearly cheap with FY EPS estimates cut about 19% in 30 days. The biggest risk is that fuel inflation and Central India dilution keep margins falling while capex of ₹3,200-3,400 cr continues, leading to further estimate cuts.

fundamental.thesis: Cohance Lifesciences is an Indian CDMO/API platform (formerly Suven Pharmaceuticals) serving global pharma innovators across Pharma CDMO, API+, Sapala nucleic-acid specialty chemicals, and Formulations — a niche franchise currently navigating a sharp operational trough driven by post-merger NJ Bio consolidation, Pharma CDMO order phasing, and Specialty Chemicals destocking. Q1FY27 consolidated revenue declined 23.1% YoY to ₹422 cr (decelerating sharply from +12.5% in Q1FY26 and extending the -13.1% full-year FY26 decline), with Pharma CDMO down 38.7% YoY, NJ Bio contributing an EBITDA loss of ₹328 mn, and PAT swinging to ₹-45 cr (-176% YoY); EBITDA margins imploded 2,220bps to 2.2%, though gross margins held at 71.5% and FCF remained a healthy ₹106 cr — indicating the trough is volume/timing-driven rather than structural margin destruction, and management has guided Q1FY27 as the floor with H2FY27 YoY recovery. Using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick per sector card guidance for a capital-intensive CDMO, the stock trades at 39.3× (P81 vs broad-market peers, 68% premium to median 23.3×), expensive on any normalised basis; trailing P/E of 88.6× (P91, distorted by the trough PAT) and forward P/E of 38.9× still sit well above sector Pharma medians of 28–40×, while sell-side FY EPS estimates have been cut 25.5% in the last 30 days — suggesting the recovery the market is paying for is actively being revised downward. The biggest risk is binary: an active FDA Warning Letter at the Nacharam FDF facility, if not resolved swiftly, could trigger customer qualification audits across the CDMO business precisely when the recovery pipeline depends on securing and delivering new orders against a backdrop of dangerously high Debt/Equity of 9.93.

Indegene sells outsourced medical, regulatory and commercial services to global biopharma clients, earning about 75% of Q2 FY27 revenue from the US (Rs 836 cr, +49.3% YoY), so it does not carry FDA manufacturing risk the way a drugmaker does. Revenue growth has stepped up from +14.8% in H1 FY26 to +39.5% in Q2 FY27 (Rs 1,122 cr), but it was flat against Q1's +39.7%, and profit has lagged: Q2 PAT rose 10.0% to Rs 112 cr, H1 PAT rose only 4.6%, and EBITDA margin fell from 21.6% in H1 FY26 to 18.5% in H1 FY27, with Q2 at 16.7% versus 19.1% in Q1. On EV/EBITDA, the main yardstick because the sector card names none for a services firm, the stock looks fair at 17.8x (P34 against a broad-market median of 23.3x, a weak comparison set), and trailing P/E of 31.2x sits inside the 28-40x pharma benchmark, but the 19.6x forward P/E relies on a profit recovery that margins do not yet show; the 4.6 debt/equity reading looks like a percentage given Rs 100 cr of net cash, and the consensus upside of +8.2% does not reconcile with the roughly Rs 515 price implied by market cap, so I gave neither any weight. The biggest risk is that growth keeps failing to reach profit and cash, since H1 operating cash flow was about Rs -1 cr against Rs 228 cr of PAT, compared with a healthy 1.62x CFO/PAT in FY26.

The biggest risk is that cost pressures (crude rising, competitive intensity in RAC) persist through FY27, making the earnings recovery priced into the forward multiple elusive and triggering a de-rating in a premium-multiple name where any guidance miss historically compresses valuation 25–40%.

fundamental.thesis: Crompton is one of India's largest fan, pump and small-appliance makers. It leads the market in ceiling fans, reaches about 2.5 lakh retailers, and gained share across most categories between FY23 and FY26 (water heaters +200 bps, residential pumps +180 bps). In Q1 FY27 revenue rose 11.8% YoY to ₹2,235 cr and PAT rose about 15% to ₹143 cr (PAT margin 6.4%), up from +7.3% revenue growth in Q3 FY26. But EBITDA margin slipped from about 11% to about 10%, because the company passed on only about 80% of cost inflation despite 10–15% price hikes, and it lost roughly ₹200 cr of primary sales to supply disruption. Trailing P/E is not meaningful because FY26 swung to a ₹-242 cr loss. On the yardsticks I used instead, the stock looks fair to slightly cheap: forward P/E is 23.9x, close to the broad-market median of 23.2x and well below the 60–100x the sector card cites for consumer names, and EV/EBITDA is 20.0x, 14% below the median. However, P/B of 6.0x is above the median, and FY EPS estimates were cut 2.6% over the last 30 days. The biggest caution is that the Q2 FY27 results filed on 2026-10-16 have not been extracted yet, so this view rests on one clean quarter after a loss-making FY26, and several snapshot fields look wrong (113% dividend yield, 5.8 debt/equity for an asset-light business with negative working capital).

fundamental.thesis: Brainbees Solutions (FIRSTCRY) is India's largest omni-channel baby-and-kids products platform, operating through firstcry.com, ~900 own stores, and the GlobalBees brand aggregator, occupying a near-monopoly position in organised baby retail — but it remains firmly pre-profit with no filed guidance on a profitability timeline. Revenue growth has decelerated from +18.2% in FY25 to +11.4% in H1FY26, and EBITDA margin has contracted from 5.0% to 4.6% over the same window; PAT margin improved marginally (-3.5% to -3.0%) but yfinance quarterly data (sanity-check only) shows losses widening sequentially from -₹28.4 cr (Q3FY26) to -₹31.2 cr (Q1FY27), consistent with the alarming 85% downward EPS estimate revision in the last 30 days. Using EV/sales as the correct yardstick for a pre-profit platform (per sector card), the stock sits at a superficially low 1.24× sales near its 52-week floor, but EV/EBITDA at 159× ranks P100 — most expensive in the 472-stock universe — with contracting unit economics and no credible bridge to positive EBIT, making the current price expensive regardless of the headline P/S cheapness. The combination of decelerating topline growth, compressing EBITDA margins, a proposed IPO-proceeds utilisation variation (governance red flag), an exchange query on abnormal volume, 29.76× debt/equity, and a RISK_OFF macro backdrop with negative Consumer Discr. sector tilt leaves the risk/reward deeply unfavourable at this stage.

fundamental.thesis: JSW Dulux (formerly Akzo Nobel India, now owned by JSW Paints since December 2025) is a mid-sized maker of decorative and industrial paints, and it is gaining market share in a crowded field. In Q1FY27 consolidated revenue fell 2.8% YoY to ₹965 cr and PAT fell 12.4% to ₹80 cr, a PAT margin of 8.3%. Margins have shrunk over the trend window: EBITDA margin went from 16.5% to 13.5% to 11.9%, and PAT margin from 10.5% to 9.2% to 8.3%. Part of the fall comes from selling the Powder Coatings division, and management reports about 25% volume growth on the business it kept, but price increases are not fully covering higher raw-material costs. On valuation, the 7.5x trailing P/E is not meaningful because it is inflated by the one-time gain from selling the divisions; using forward P/E and P/B instead, 31.3x forward and 6.0x book are a discount to the usual 40–60x paints premium but not a bargain, with the stock mid-range in its 52-week band, so I grade it fair. The biggest risks are crude near $99 and rising, which feeds directly into paint input costs, and analysts who have cut EPS estimates by about 8–9% over 90 days.

IndiaMART runs a large online B2B marketplace, with 8.9 million supplier storefronts and 217 thousand paying suppliers, and earns mainly from advance-paid subscriptions (deferred revenue of ₹2,029 cr, 4.7x quarterly revenue). In Q2 FY27, revenue rose about 10% YoY to ₹429 cr, slowing from +12% a year earlier, while PAT rose about 10% to ₹91 cr and EBITDA margin improved from 33% to 37%; however, PAT margin was flat at about 21.2% on reported figures, not 'expanding' as the trend table suggests, and Q1 FY27 and Q3 FY26 data are missing, so the trajectory is only partly visible. Valuation is fair using EV/EBITDA and EV/sales for a profitable platform: EV/EBITDA of 18.1x and trailing P/E of 27.1x sit about 22-23% below the broad-market median (P34-P35), but the peer set is not a close match, and P/E rises to about 35x on annualised Q2 PAT, though net cash of roughly ₹3,234 cr (about 25% of market cap) gives some cushion. The biggest risk is that paying suppliers fell 2% YoY and collections grew only 9%, which suggests growth increasingly relies on higher revenue per supplier and could slow further; the sell-side +30.7% upside is also unreliable because the implied price of about ₹1,483 conflicts with the 52-week range of ₹1,911-2,799 and the roughly ₹2,137 implied by the range position.

fundamental.thesis: Sapphire Foods runs KFC and Pizza Hut restaurants in India and Sri Lanka (974 stores as of Q1 FY26) and is being merged into Devyani International at 177 DIL shares for every 100 SAPPHIRE shares, so the stock now largely trades as a proxy for DEVYANI. The latest extracted figures are stale (FY26; the Q2 FY27 results filed on 2026-10-22 are not in the dataset). They show revenue growth slowing from +13.0% (Q4FY25) to about +8% in every period since, PAT moving from a small profit to a loss of about -1.0% of revenue, and same-store sales of 0% at KFC and -8% at Pizza Hut. That means growth is coming almost entirely from new stores, not from more sales per store. Trailing P/E is not meaningful because the company is loss-making, so I graded valuation on EV/EBITDA: 27.8x is only slightly above the broad-market median of 23.3x (P61), which is fair for a QSR operator. Forward P/E of 96x (P99) and next-year EPS estimates cut by 21% in 30 days show earnings are not catching up with the price. The biggest risk is weak same-store sales combined with falling earnings estimates ahead of a merger swap that ties the stock's value to Devyani's own derating risk.

fundamental.thesis: Swiggy is India's number-two food-delivery and quick-commerce (Instamart) platform, with a small but fast-growing out-of-home dining segment. Revenue keeps growing in the mid-30s: H1 FY27 rose 36.7% to ₹14,383 cr, and the implied Q2 is about ₹7,571 cr, up roughly 36% YoY, slower than FY26's +51.4%. The trend-table label 'accelerating' mixes half-year, full-year and quarterly periods and overstates the move. Losses are narrowing on a YoY basis: the H1 EBITDA loss fell to ₹997 cr from ₹1,606 cr and H1 net loss to ₹1,713 cr from ₹2,289 cr. Sequentially, however, the Q2 loss widened to about ₹922 cr from ₹791 cr in Q1. Food delivery is close to breakeven at a -7.65% margin, but Instamart still lost ₹1,415 cr at a -55.9% margin. Because P/E and EV/EBITDA are meaningless while the company is loss-making, I graded valuation on EV/sales plus unit-economics delivery, as the sector card prescribes for platforms. Price/sales of 2.89x (about 2.3x on annualised H1 revenue) and P/B of 3.35x (P37 vs the broad market) look fair, not stretched, for ~36% growth with improving margins. Sell-side estimates have been revised sharply upward (FY EPS +50.7% over 90 days), but there is no formal management guidance, and the main risk is that the Instamart cash burn in the quick-commerce price war delays group profitability.

fundamental.thesis: Urban Company is India's largest online platform for home services such as beauty, cleaning and repairs, and it also sells its own water purifiers and smart locks (Native), runs international operations and has a Saudi joint venture. It is now funding a heavily loss-making quick home-help business called InstaHelp. Q2FY27 revenue was ₹537 cr, up 41% YoY, faster than FY26's +36%. Orders rose 103% and Net Transaction Value (NTV, the total value of services booked) rose 39% to ₹1,432 cr. Profit went the other way: consolidated adjusted EBITDA was -₹144 cr, a -26.8% margin, against +6.8% for FY26. That is because InstaHelp lost ₹174 cr, which wiped out a core business that is profitable and improving (core EBITDA ₹30 cr, up 213% YoY; India consumer margin 3.5%, up 110 bps). Since the business is pre-profit, P/E means nothing here, so I graded valuation on price-to-sales and unit economics instead. At 12.3x sales and 8.6x book value (76th percentile of the broad market), the price is reasonable for 40% growth only if InstaHelp's losses keep shrinking. InstaHelp's loss per order did improve 19% from the previous quarter but is still ₹279. I rate valuation fair, not cheap. The biggest risk is that the InstaHelp cash burn continues while the newly approved ₹2,500 cr capital raise dilutes shareholders, in a risk-off market that punishes high-multiple loss-makers.

fundamental.thesis: Zee Entertainment is India's second-largest broadcast media group (~50 TV channels plus the ZEE5 OTT platform), structurally pressured by the secular migration to streaming and left exposed after the Jiostar/Sony merger collapsed; it now carries substantial governance and legal overhangs that suppress any re-rating. FY26 annual revenue declined 1.9% YoY to ₹7,567 Cr while PAT collapsed 82.8% to ₹120 Cr, compressing PAT margin to 1.6% and EBITDA margin to a catastrophic 2.6% (from 13.4% in FY25) — the multi-quarter trajectory shows revenue decelerating and margins contracting across every available period with no stabilisation evident in filings. Forward P/E of 13.42× (P19 vs broad-market peers, -42% below median) and P/B of 0.9× (P2 vs peers, -80% below median) both screen as unambiguously cheap; EV/EBITDA of 23× looks deceptively at median but is computed on severely depressed EBITDA — on normalised 12-13% margins the implied EV/EBITDA would be sub-5×, confirming franchise-level cheapness if operational recovery is achievable. The single largest risk to the recovery thesis is the IDBI Bank insolvency petition (filed September 2025) seeking NCLT-admitted CIRP initiation, which if granted would be existential for the business regardless of underlying brand and content-IP value.

Ather Energy is a pure-play premium electric two-wheeler maker with 15.1% market share, down from 17.2% a year ago, and 15% of revenue comes from non-vehicle sources. In Q2FY27, revenue rose 62.8% YoY to Rs 1,464 cr on 42% higher volumes and 14.6% higher revenue per unit, compared with +53% in Q3FY26 and +66% for FY26, while PAT improved from a Rs 154 cr loss to a Rs 1.26 cr profit and EBITDA margin moved from -3.0% in Q3FY26 to 5.0%, although the missing Q1FY27 row and mixed annual and quarterly periods make the 'accelerating' signal unreliable. Valuation is expensive using the pre-profit yardstick of EV/sales proxied by P/S, growth delivery and unit economics rather than trailing P/E: P/S is 15.5x (about 11x annualised Q2 revenue), forward P/E is 374x, and the stock is near its 52-week high with the mean target about level with the price, though EV/EBITDA is not meaningful, no tight peer set is available, and the price inputs and 25.82 debt/equity figure look inconsistent or unclear and were given little weight. The biggest risk is that aluminium, copper and memory-chip cost inflation interrupts margin gains while share is falling, a concern supported by next-FY EPS estimates being cut 49% in 30 days even as all 12 analysts stay at buy.

fundamental.thesis: JBM Auto combines a components business (Q2FY27 revenue about Rs 1,037 cr, +24.7% YoY) with a fast-growing electric bus business (about Rs 548 cr, +21.8% YoY, 24% reported market share and 578 buses delivered in the quarter). Reported revenue growth has accelerated from +8.6% in Q2FY26 to +16.2% in Q3FY26 and +21.1% to Rs 1,656 cr in Q2FY27, with PAT up 12.5% to Rs 59 cr, but PAT margin has slipped from 3.9% to 3.6% to 3.5%; Q1FY27 and FY26 data are missing, and the table's Q2FY26 revenue and PAT imply lower growth of about +17.7% and +7.3%, so the acceleration is less certain than it looks. Using EV/EBITDA as the main yardstick for this capital-intensive business, valuation is expensive at 24.0x for a 12.2% EBITDA margin, even though that is only P52 against a broad-market peer set rather than close auto peers; trailing P/E of 64.8x is well above the 18-30x OEM range, P/B of 12.7x is P89, and forward P/E of 31.0x assumes earnings roughly double. The biggest risk is that growth keeps needing debt-funded capital while thin margins and weak cash generation (H1FY27 operating cash flow Rs 143 cr, free cash flow Rs 14 cr, net debt Rs 2,732 cr) leave little room for error; the 14.0% dividend yield looks like a data error and was ignored, and the '2.7x H1 revenue' debt figure is wrong because Rs 2,732 cr is about 0.9x H1 revenue.

fundamental.thesis: UltraTech is India's largest cement maker with 210.1 mtpa of capacity, and it benefits from an industry where it and Adani now control roughly 45% of capacity, which supports pricing discipline. In Q2FY27 revenue grew 18.9% YoY to ₹23,024 cr, up from 15.8% in Q1, and PAT rose 21.3% to ₹1,501 cr on 12.9% volume growth. Margins fell sharply from Q1, though: EBITDA margin dropped from 20.9% to 16.6% and PAT margin from 10.6% to 6.5%, and EBITDA per tonne fell from ₹1,214 to ₹974 (still up ₹60 YoY). The cause is cost inflation, with fuel up 14% and packing bags up 30% on the crude spike, against realisation growth of only 2%. Part of this is the normal monsoon-quarter slowdown, and H1 cash conversion is solid at 1.68x CFO/PAT. Using the cement yardstick (EBITDA per tonne plus peer multiples, since live EV/EBITDA was not available), the stock looks fair. Its 39.6x trailing P/E is close to the sector median of 37.3x (P53 among peers), but the 4.5x P/B is rich for a 10.6% ROE, and the 25.1x forward P/E rests on estimates that have been cut 11–13% in the last 30 days. The biggest risk is that crude above $103 keeps fuel and packing costs high while realisations barely rise, so per-tonne profits stay squeezed and the stock de-rates as analysts keep trimming earnings.

fundamental.thesis: Lloyds Metals and Energy is a vertically integrated mining-steel-MDO (Mine Developer & Operator) company with captive iron ore giving it structural margin advantages; Q1FY27 revenue surged 208.6% YoY to ₹7,354 cr as the steel segment scaled (+616% YoY) and MDO volumes grew, with EBITDA margins expanding sharply to 40.0% (vs 29.6% in FY25) and PAT rising 165.9% YoY to ₹1,734 cr — the multi-quarter trajectory is consistently accelerating across revenue, EBITDA, and PAT margins over six periods. Using EV/EBITDA as the primary yardstick per the sector card for capital-intensive businesses, the 19.1× multiple sits well above the 5–8× mid-cycle range for commodity steel cyclicals, but the forward P/E of 12.06× (P15 vs broad-market peers, with analyst EPS estimates revised +38% in the last 30/90 days) reflects a substantial earnings step-up already in the price, and the captive-mine model's 40%+ EBITDA margins are structurally superior to a pure-play mill — grading as fair with the stock near 84.3% of its 52-week range limiting margin of safety. The biggest risk is elevated leverage (~₹21,204 cr total debt, D/E ~1.33× per Q1FY27 filings, current ratio 0.84×, FCF deeply negative at −₹1,853 cr in FY26) alongside a loss-making copper segment, which would be acutely stressed if steel spreads or mining volumes soften.

fundamental.thesis: NMDC Steel is a government-controlled (50.79% GoI stake) integrated steel producer demerged from NMDC Ltd, operating a greenfield Nagarnar plant and currently awaiting a strategic disinvestment buyer — creating a persistent ownership overhang. Q1FY27 revenue grew 8.8% YoY to ₹3,662cr, a sharp deceleration from +72.4% in 9MFY26 and +178.9% in FY25, but the critical directional story is the margin turnaround: PAT margin has expanded from −35.8% (Q3FY25) through −3.4% (9MFY26) to +1.4% (Q1FY27) as the greenfield plant ramps utilisation and fixed-cost absorption improves. Using EV/EBITDA — the correct yardstick for a capital-intensive steel cyclical — NSLNISP trades at 11.69× versus the broad-market median of 23.3×, placing it at P17 (cheap), and P/B of 1.05× puts it at P3; the 235× trailing P/E is a pure distortion of near-zero earnings and must not be read as 'expensive', but D/E of 35× and a DSCR of only 0.17 mean the company cannot comfortably service its own debt and any spread compression could tip it back to losses. The single biggest risk is that extreme financial leverage leaves no margin of safety against rising crude costs (a direct input-cost headwind in the current macro), a weakening rupee, and the prolonged disinvestment uncertainty that suppresses any rerating.

fundamental.thesis: Nuvoco Vistas is an East- and North-focused cement and ready-mix concrete (RMC) maker with about 35 MTPA of target capacity. It is a mid-tier player in a sector where UltraTech and Adani now control about 45% of capacity. Using the filings trend table (the yfinance rows are inconsistent and were ignored), Q2FY27 revenue rose 13.5% YoY to ₹2,790 cr, up from +9.0% in Q1, and cement volumes grew 9% YoY against 5% in Q1. Profit quality is thinner than the headline suggests. PAT rose 78% YoY, but only to ₹65 cr, a 2.3% margin. EBITDA margin fell to 14.7% from 18.3% in Q1 and 15.1% a year ago. Implied EBITDA per tonne is about ₹875, below the healthy ₹900–1,100 band and down from roughly ₹1,080 in Q1. Valuation is graded on EV/EBITDA, the right yardstick for a capital-intensive cement maker, not P/E. At 8.6x (P8 of the broad market, no close peers in the universe), with P/B of 1.09x, forward P/E of 20.5x against trailing 31x, and the price at 18% of its 52-week range, the stock looks cheap against typical cement multiples. Much of that discount is justified by an ROE of only 3.7% and high debt. The biggest risk is the balance sheet. Net debt is ₹5,028 cr, current ratio is 0.57x, free cash flow was -₹246 cr in H1 because of capex, and legal disputes are pending: the ₹490 cr CCI penalty and about ₹454 cr of West Bengal incentive provisions. These come on top of rising crude and a weak rupee pushing up fuel and freight costs.

Abbott India is the listed Indian arm of a global healthcare group and sells mainly branded medicines in India, the sector card's 'safe template' with no direct exposure to the US tariff on patented drugs. The only official figures available are full-year FY26: revenue ₹6,929 cr (+8.1% YoY) and PAT ₹1,552 cr (+9.7% YoY), giving a healthy 22.4% PAT margin, but cash conversion was only 0.85x CFO/PAT. Q1FY27 has not been extracted from filings, and the yfinance quarterly rows (about ₹930 cr per quarter) do not reconcile with the annual total, so quarterly direction cannot be verified and I have ignored those rows. On trailing P/E, the right yardstick for an India branded-formulations company, the stock trades at 35.8x. That sits inside the 28–40x pharma range, so valuation is fair, with forward P/E of 28.8x implying expected earnings growth and the price near its 52-week low (8.4% of range) offering a better entry point. The ratio feed looks unreliable (a 201% dividend yield and D/E of 3.6 are implausible for this cash-rich company), and the key near-term risk is the Q2FY27 result on 5 Nov, which could confirm or break the steady high-single-digit growth story.

fundamental.thesis: Anthem Biosciences is a contract research, development and manufacturing (CRDMO) business, with CRDMO at 84% of H1 FY27 revenue and specialty ingredients at 16%, plus a net cash position of Rs 1,538 cr. H1 FY27 revenue fell 7.2% YoY to Rs 1,012 cr while PAT rose 7.2% to Rs 331 cr, but the quarters diverge: revenue fell 22.6% in Q1 and recovered about 7.8% in Q2 to about Rs 594 cr (derived from H1 less Q1), with Q2 PAT up 21.9% to Rs 211.5 cr, so growth has slowed from FY26's +15% and one rebound quarter in a lumpy business does not yet confirm a trend. On EV/EBITDA, the main yardstick here alongside growth delivery, the stock is expensive at 50.8x (P89 and 118% above the broad-market median, with no tight peer set available), and its 76.2x trailing P/E is also well above the 28-40x pharma range, leaving little room for error. The biggest risk is a de-rating if growth does not recover enough to justify the multiple, as 90-day EPS estimates have been trimmed (-1.4% this year, -3.6% next year) despite 8 of 8 analysts rating it a buy, and the data provided has no contract-pipeline figures to support the recovery.

Aster DM Healthcare, now rebranded as Aster DM Quality Care after combining with the CARE Hospitals platform, is a south-India-focused multi-specialty hospital chain whose earnings come from occupancy, revenue per bed and new bed additions. The latest usable quarter is stale: in Q3 FY26 revenue was ₹1,186 cr, up 12.9% YoY, but PAT fell 7.6% to ₹52 cr and PAT margin compressed to 4.4%, against 8.6% in H1 FY26 and 8.5% for FY26. The Q1 FY27 rows came back blank, and Q2 FY27 results are not due until the 6 Nov board meeting, so the current trajectory cannot be confirmed and the pre-computed 'accelerating' signal compares mismatched periods and is not reliable. On valuation I used EV/EBITDA as the yardstick, since hospitals are capital-intensive and recently merged. At 45.9x EV/EBITDA, about 97% above the broad-market median, 123x trailing P/E, 8.9x P/B against only 10.1% ROE, and the price at 85% of its 52-week range, the stock is expensive even allowing for the usual hospital premium. The 41x forward P/E shows that the market already expects sharp earnings growth from the merger. The biggest risk is that merger integration or new-bed ramp-up costs keep margins depressed while the stock is priced for delivery; fiscal-year EPS estimates were already cut 5% in the last 30 days even though 11 of 12 analysts rate it a buy.

Profit is lagging revenue: implied Q2 PAT of about ₹68 cr grew only around 6% YoY, down from +33% in Q1, and implied Q2 EBITDA margin fell to roughly 29% from 37.5% in Q1, partly from losses at the US subsidiary Stellon and the newly acquired Celliimune. Using trailing P/E as the yardstick, 50.8x sits well above the 28–40x pharma range, and EV/EBITDA of 37x ranks at P78 of the broad market, so the stock is expensive even after the forward P/E falls to 34x; the main risk is that margin compression continues while the market prices a full earnings recovery.

fundamental.thesis: CEAT is India's #4 tyre maker (global rank #4 by brand) with 51% replacement, 30% OEM, and 19% export mix, operating at 95% capacity utilisation across ~80,000 daily tyres — a capital-intensive ancillary with defensive replacement demand. The main risks are weak cash conversion (H1 free cash flow was -₹263 cr, with operating cash flow at -0.04x PAT) and a slow Europe business. Analysts keep cutting estimates (FY EPS down 2.3% over 90 days) even though 4 of 5 rate it a buy, and rising crude in a risk-off market is a headwind for auto demand.

The biggest risk is that debt is likely collateralised against the Britannia stake, meaning a sustained FII-driven de-rating of Britannia under the current RISK_OFF regime could trigger a collateral squeeze at the BBTC level, amplifying downside disproportionately.

At trailing P/E of 54.93×, Bikaji sits within the FMCG sector benchmark of 40–65× and is graded FAIR; the forward P/E of 39.26× implies ~40% earnings recovery is already priced in, but the stock is at 0.4% of its 52-week range (near lows) and sell-side EPS estimates have been cut -5.5% over 90 days despite unanimous buy ratings — a pre-derating warning the data feed does not yet reflect in targets. The biggest risk is that sustained margin compression combined with falling estimates converts into earnings misses in Q2FY27 onward, triggering multiple derating from elevated multiples alongside an elevated debt/equity load (17.53× as flagged, though seemingly inconsistent with modest finance costs of ₹5 cr/quarter and warrants verification against filings).

fundamental.thesis: CCL Products is one of the world's largest private-label instant coffee makers, with plants in India and Vietnam (Ngon Coffee, which earned ₹53 cr PAT in Q2 alone), plus a small but growing branded domestic business; it trades as FMCG but is mostly a B2B coffee processor exposed to green-coffee price swings. Revenue growth has slowed sharply, from +44.5% (H1FY26) and +38.5% (Q3FY26) to +13.7% in Q1FY27 and +10.5% for H1FY27 (₹2,411 cr). That implies Q2FY27 grew only about +7–8% (≈₹1,211 cr vs ≈₹1,127 cr), most likely as coffee-price pass-through fades. Profits are still growing much faster than sales: H1 PAT is up 42.5% to ₹247 cr, PAT margin has widened from 8.0% to 10.2%, and cash conversion is strong (H1 CFO/PAT 1.78x, FCF ₹414 cr). Valuation is fair rather than cheap. I used EV/EBITDA because this is a capital- and working-capital-heavy processor, not a classic staples brand: EV/EBITDA is 21.6x (P46 vs market) and trailing P/E is 38.9x, at the bottom of the FMCG 40–60x band but rich for a commodity-linked exporter. Forward P/E of 24.1x already prices in strong earnings growth, and the stock sits at 77% of its 52-week range. The biggest risk is that revenue growth keeps slowing toward single digits as coffee prices normalise, while margin gains, which drove most of this year's profit growth, become harder to repeat.

Emami is a mid-sized Indian personal-care and OTC/healthcare FMCG company (Navratna, BoroPlus, Zandu, Kesh King) with strong niche brands, and it has just completed a buyback that extinguished 73 lakh shares. The latest reliable numbers from official filings show FY26 revenue of about ₹3,780 cr, down 0.8% YoY, and PAT of ₹775 cr, down 3.4%, with a 20.5% PAT margin. Quarterly growth has been choppy and has not shown a clear trend: Q3FY26 grew 9.8% while H1FY26 fell 5.2%. EBITDA margin has eased from the Q3 peak of 38.9% to 27.7% for the year, while gross margin held steady at around 70%. Q1FY27 extraction is missing, the Q2 FY26 row is clearly corrupt and is ignored, and Q2 FY27 results are not yet in the data. Using the P/E yardstick the FMCG card prescribes, trailing P/E of 22.5x (forward 18.5x, EV/EBITDA 17.7x) sits well below the sector's normal 40-65x band, so the stock grades cheap, and it trades near its 52-week low. However, the sector card warns that cheap FMCG usually signals a structural growth problem, and flat revenue with high ad spend (19.6% of revenue) fits that pattern. The biggest risk is that the core domestic business keeps stalling on volumes while sell-side earnings estimates are still being cut (-5.2% over 90 days), which would turn the low multiple into a value trap rather than a re-rating.

fundamental.thesis: Godfrey Phillips India is India's second-largest cigarette maker (Philip Morris-affiliated) with a growing FMCG business, commanding a dominant position in the premium cigarette segment. Q1FY27 revenue surged 110.6% YoY to ₹3,820 cr — likely reflecting inclusion of low-margin tobacco leaf trading — but PAT collapsed 44.3% YoY to ₹198 cr as PAT margin compressed sharply from 19.7% to 5.2%, a severe quality-of-earnings deterioration that makes the revenue acceleration misleading. At trailing P/E of 23.2×, the stock trades at a 34% discount to the broad market median and well below the FMCG sector norm of 40–65×, placing it in the 'cheap' band by sector yardstick — however, tobacco names structurally attract a regulatory/ESG discount globally, and if the underlying PAT margin has genuinely structurally compressed (FY26 CFO/PAT only 0.34×), the apparent cheapness may be a value trap. The biggest risk is that normalized earnings power is now materially lower than the headline trailing figure implies, and high leverage (D/E 3.76×) leaves little cushion if the margin recovery does not materialize.

fundamental.thesis: Patanjali Foods is India's largest edible oils company (formerly Ruchi Soya), with a fast-growing FMCG overlay spanning biscuits, nutrition, and home/personal care under the Patanjali brand — but edible oils still account for roughly 70%+ of revenues, making this a commodity-FMCG hybrid rather than a pure compounder, and that matters critically for how to frame the valuation. Q1FY27 delivered record revenue of ₹11,337 cr (+29.3% YoY, accelerating from +20.9% in Q2FY26) and PAT of ₹336 cr (+86.1% YoY), but underlying quality is deteriorating: gross margin compressed from 15.26% (Q2FY26) to 13.42% (Q1FY27), EBITDA margin fell from 6.2% to 4.8%, and PAT margin contracted to 3.0% — a persistent multi-quarter contraction signal that runs counter to the top-line acceleration. At trailing P/E 25.43×, the stock screens cheap versus the FMCG sector benchmark of 40–60×, but the discount is structurally warranted by the commodity-heavy business mix; EV/EBITDA of 25× (P55 vs broad-market peers) and P/E peer rank of P32 both point to fair value rather than genuine mispricing, and the sector card's own caution — 'cheap FMCG usually means a structural problem' — applies directly here. The overriding risk is extreme balance sheet leverage (D/E 21.3×) combined with negative FCF (CFO/PAT −1.13× in Q2FY26) — at a 5.29% US 10Y yield and with PAT margins at 3%, any commodity cost spike or interest burden increase could rapidly destroy earnings entirely.

Radico Khaitan is one of India's largest spirits makers, known for premium brands like Magic Moments and Rampur, and benefits from the premiumisation trend in alcohol. Q2FY27 gross revenue was about ₹5,583 cr, up 10.4% YoY, but growth has slowed from +29.4% in Q2FY26 and +24.7% in FY26 to +10.4% in each of the last two periods, while PAT jumped roughly 66% YoY to about ₹232 cr (H1 PAT ₹462 cr, +71%) as margins expanded and net debt fell to ₹175 cr. On the FMCG yardstick of trailing P/E (sector card norm 40–65×), the stock is expensive at 81.8× trailing P/E and 40.3× EV/EBITDA, sits at about 96% of its 52-week range, and ranks around P89–P93 against the broad market; the 51× forward P/E and sell-side EPS upgrades of +19% over 90 days support earnings momentum but leave little room for a miss. The biggest risk is a de-rating if revenue growth keeps slowing toward single digits while the price already assumes continued strong profit growth, and a 'Change in Management' filing on 2026-10-27 has not yet been assessed.

Cyient is a mid-cap engineering-services firm with three businesses: design and engineering services (DET, about 74% of revenue), electronics contract manufacturing (DLM), and a loss-making semiconductor unit, and it recently bought TAO Digital for about ₹2,156 cr. H1 FY27 revenue grew 23.4% YoY to ₹4,311 cr, but that growth is largely acquisition-driven, and PAT fell 19.7% YoY to ₹241 cr, so the PAT margin dropped from 8.6% to 5.6%. Profit has now fallen in every reported period (-24.9% in Q3FY26, -32.3% in Q1FY27, -19.7% in H1FY27), and the semiconductor unit lost ₹58 cr at a -16.5% margin. On valuation, I used P/E and EV/EBITDA together, and the stock looks fair rather than cheap: trailing P/E of 22.6x sits at the bottom of the 22–30x IT range, and EV/EBITDA of 11.4x ranks P16 against the broad market, but ROE is only 7.8%. The low 11.9x forward P/E rests on analyst estimates that were cut 18% over the last 90 days, so it should not be trusted yet. The biggest risk is that semiconductor losses and integrating TAO keep eating into the steady DET profits, and the data has gaps: the yfinance Q2 revenue of ₹1,498 cr conflicts with the filings, Q1FY27 shows two different growth rates, and the reported debt/equity and dividend-yield figures look like data errors.
